final_answer:
Probably not. Under Texas law the trial court most likely did not err in disqualifying Smith Fullingham.

Framework. Texas treats a nonlawyer (paralegal or legal assistant) who switches sides in the same matter differently from a lawyer. Two presumptions apply. First, an irrebuttable presumption that the nonlawyer obtained the former client's confidences while working on the matter. Jones's deposition testimony (several hundred privileged communications, strategy meetings, preparing litigation documents) satisfies this, so Apex does not have to prove what she actually knows. Second, a presumption that the nonlawyer shared those confidences with the new firm. This is ordinarily rebuttable, because courts do not want to unduly restrict nonlawyer mobility. The firm can rebut it by showing it took sufficient precautions: it instructed her not to work on the matter and took other reasonable steps to shield her from it (In re American Home Products; Phoenix Founders v. Marshall; In re Columbia Valley Healthcare, Tex. 2010).

Why the rebuttable route fails here. Columbia Valley holds that the second presumption becomes irrebuttable, and disqualification of the firm is required, if the nonlawyer actually works on the same matter at the new firm at the firm's direction, where the firm reasonably should know of the conflict. In re Turner (Tex. 2017) applied this to a paralegal who worked on the matter at the new firm, even in a largely clerical role, and after the firm took remedial steps once the conflict was raised. Jones worked on the Apex-Prestige dispute with a Smith Fullingham attorney on thirteen occasions from 2017 to 2022 and e-filed two documents in March 2022 under her own name. Her work was limited and secretarial, but that does not matter, because Texas does not ask whether the work was substantive. The firm also did nothing at hiring: it never asked about her prior work, and it screened her only in 2023, after Apex raised the issue. A screen put in place after she had already worked on the matter, and after the conflict was raised, does not cure the problem. The firm's reliance on her claim that she does not recall her prior work, and on her statement that she shared nothing, fails against the irrebuttable presumptions. Her lack of recall is not a safe harbor either, because the test is the presumption of what she learned, not her present memory, and the firm should have asked her when she was hired, since it knew the Apex-Prestige case was pending at the firm. The 'should have known' element is therefore easily met.

Timeliness and waiver. A party that delays unreasonably in moving to disqualify can waive the complaint (In re EPIC Holdings; Vaughan v. Walther). Apex learned of Jones's role in January 2023 and moved in early March 2023, roughly two months later after inquiring and receiving the firm's response. That is a short delay with a reasonable explanation. The earlier thirteen occasions and the 2022 filings were not known to Apex, so there was no earlier apparent conflict. Waiver is unlikely.

Standard of review and other considerations. Disqualification is a severe remedy, and mandamus is the usual vehicle. A court abuses its discretion if it misapplies the law. Because Texas law required disqualification on these facts, an abuse of discretion argument by Smith Fullingham is weak. Possible counterarguments: the work was minimal; the prejudice or tactical-motive concerns raised in some Texas cases; a 2017 return that followed a four-year gap. None is likely to change the result under Columbia Valley/Turner, because the rule is prophylactic and does not require proof of actual disclosure.

Caveats. I could not retrieve full text of the opinions because the fetch tool was blocked for the court and aggregator sites. The holdings above are based on search-result excerpts of those opinions, so pin cites and some details (including whether the Texas Supreme Court has refined the rule after Turner) are unverified. I did not verify the current text of the Texas Disciplinary Rules.

claims.text: Texas applies an irrebuttable presumption that a side-switching nonlawyer obtained confidences, and a presumption she shared them with the new firm, generally rebuttable by adequate shielding.

Where the nonlawyer actually works on the same matter at the new firm and the firm reasonably should know of the conflict, the sharing presumption is irrebuttable and disqualification is required, even for limited clerical work.

Jones's thirteen work occasions and two filings, no inquiry at hiring, and screening only after Apex's objection do not avert disqualification; her claimed lack of recall does not rebut the presumptions.
Apex's roughly two-month delay after learning of Jones's role was reasonable and unlikely to be waiver.
Disqualification is a severe remedy reviewed for abuse of discretion, but misapplying the law is an abuse; here the order is consistent with the law.
